title: The Enlightenment
bullets: Voltaire, Locke, and Rousseau challenged the authority of kings and churches across Europe.
The Encyclopédie cataloged human knowledge and spread Enlightenment ideas to a wide audience.
Enlightenment thinkers placed reason above superstition in politics, science, and daily life.
Enlightenment ideals inspired revolutions in America, France, and beyond.
Enlightenment philosophers championed free speech, religious tolerance, and individual rights.
The Enlightenment peaked in 18th-century Europe and reshaped governments on both sides of the Atlantic.
Salons and coffeehouses spread radical new ideas about liberty, science, and human rights.
Enlightenment thinkers challenged absolute monarchy and helped inspire modern constitutional democracy.

title: American Revolution
hook: 1776: 13 colonies said NO to a king.
bullets: Boston Tea Party — 342 chests dumped
Declaration signed July 4 1776
Valley Forge nearly broke the army
France's alliance turned the tide
America was born 1783
Taxation without representation became the colonists' rallying cry against British rule.
The war lasted from 1775 to 1783 and forged a new republic built on Enlightenment ideals.
The Treaty of Paris in 1783 formally recognized American independence from Britain.

title: French Revolution
hook: They stormed a prison and changed EVERYTHING.
bullets: Bastille — July 14 1789
King Louis XVI guillotined
Reign of Terror
Women marched on Versailles
Liberté Egalité Fraternité
The revolution began when commoners stormed the Bastille prison on July 14, 1789.
King Louis XVI was executed by guillotine in 1793, ending over a thousand years of French monarchy.
The Reign of Terror saw thousands executed before Napoleon eventually seized power.

title: Napoleon's Rise and Fall
bullets: Austerlitz and Jena — unstoppable
Napoleonic Code still shapes law
Moscow 1812 — army froze
Escaped Elba
Waterloo ended it all
Napoleon crowned himself Emperor of France in 1804, crowning a meteoric rise from artillery officer.
His Napoleonic Code still influences legal systems across Europe and Latin America today.
Defeated at Waterloo in 1815, he was exiled to Saint Helena where he died in 1821.

title: Haitian Revolution
bullets: Only successful slave revolt in history
Toussaint Louverture led the fight
Independence Jan 1 1804
First Black republic
Terrified the world
Toussaint Louverture led enslaved people in a revolt that defeated French, British, and Spanish forces.
Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, becoming the first Black republic in the world.
France later demanded crippling reparations that kept Haiti in debt for generations.

title: Industrial Revolution
hook: Steam power changed EVERYTHING in 50 years.
bullets: Watt's steam engine 1769
Cities exploded overnight
Child labor was the norm
Luddites smashed machines
Railroads changed travel forever
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain around 1760 and spread across Europe and North America.
Factory work drew millions from farms into crowded cities, transforming society forever.
Mechanization created vast wealth but also deep inequality and harsh working conditions.

title: Lewis and Clark Expedition
bullets: St Louis to Pacific and back
Sacagawea saved the expedition
300+ species documented
50+ Native nations met
Only 1 death
President Thomas Jefferson commissioned the expedition to explore the newly acquired Louisiana Territory.
The Corps of Discovery traveled roughly 8,000 miles from St. Louis to the Pacific and back.
Their maps and journals opened the American West to settlement and trade.

title: Abolitionist Movement
hook: Am I not a man and a brother?
bullets: Britain banned slave trade 1807
Frederick Douglass — legend
Harriet Tubman — 70+ to freedom
Emancipation Proclamation 1863
Freedom was fought for daily
Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became one of America's greatest orators and writers.
Harriet Tubman's Underground Railroad helped more than 70 enslaved people reach freedom.
The movement combined moral persuasion, legal action, and direct resistance to end slavery.

title: California Gold Rush
bullets: Sutter's Mill — Jan 1848
SF: 200 to 36000 people
Most miners made NOTHING
Merchants got rich
Rivers destroyed
James Marshall discovered gold at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, sparking a global rush.
San Francisco grew from about 200 residents to 36,000 in just a few years.
Most prospectors earned little while merchants and suppliers became the real winners.

title: Darwin and Evolution
hook: One book destroyed how we see LIFE.
bullets: Origin of Species — 1859
Galapagos finches proved it
5 years on HMS Beagle
Waited 20 years to publish
Changed biology forever
Darwin spent five years aboard HMS Beagle collecting specimens across South America and the Pacific.
He waited over 20 years to publish, fearing backlash against his evolutionary theory.
On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, became the foundation of modern biology.
credit: Charles_Darwin_seated.jpg : Henry Maull (1829–1914) and John Fox (1832–… · Public domain

title: American Civil War
bullets: Antietam — deadliest day
Gettysburg Address 1863
Emancipation Proclamation
Lee surrendered 1865
The war began when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861.
An estimated 620,000 soldiers died, making it America's deadliest conflict at the time.
The Union victory in 1865 ended slavery and preserved the United States as one nation.
credit: Unknown author; Kurz & Allison, Art Publishers, Chicago, U.S.A. / Resto… · Public domain

title: Transcontinental Railroad
bullets: Completed May 10 1869
20000+ Chinese laborers
Months to 7 days coast to coast
130 million acres given away
Golden spike driven
The Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869.
More than 20,000 Chinese laborers built the treacherous western half through mountains and desert.
The railroad cut cross-country travel from months to about seven days.
credit: United States Pacific Railway Commission. Digital image reconstruction… · CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Meiji Restoration
hook: Japan feudal to world power in 40 YEARS.
bullets: 250 years of shogunate — ended
Emperor Meiji restored 1868
Samurai abolished
Beat China AND Russia
40-year transformation
The Meiji Restoration began in 1868, ending over 250 years of Tokugawa shogunate rule.
Japan rapidly adopted Western industry, military methods, and education to avoid colonization.
Within decades Japan defeated China and Russia, proving its transformation to the world.

title: Jack the Ripper
bullets: 1888 — East End London
5 murders 0 arrests
Letters signed Jack the Ripper.
No DNA. No forensics
Still unsolved
Jack the Ripper killed at least five women in London's East End during the autumn of 1888.
The killer taunted police and newspapers with letters signed 'Jack the Ripper.'
Despite massive investigation, no suspect was ever convicted and the case remains unsolved.
credit: R. Taylor (R. & E. Taylor (Firm)) · Public domain

title: Wright Brothers First Flight
bullets: Dec 17 1903 — Kitty Hawk
120 feet. 12 seconds
Bicycle shop to aviation
66 years later — Moon landing
Every plane uses their design
Orville and Wilbur Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, before teaching themselves aerodynamics.
Their Flyer achieved the first powered, controlled flight on December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk.
Their three-axis control system remains fundamental to every aircraft flying today.

title: Sinking of the Titanic
bullets: April 14 1912
1500+ died
Lifeboats for HALF the people
Band played as it sank
Warnings ignored
The Titanic struck an iceberg on April 14, 1912, and sank in roughly three hours.
Of the 2,240 passengers and crew aboard, more than 1,500 lost their lives in the icy Atlantic.
The disaster led to major reforms in maritime safety, including mandatory lifeboats for all.
credit: Francis Godolphin Osbourne Stuart · Public domain

title: World War I
bullets: Franz Ferdinand shot — 1914
Trench warfare = hell
Poison gas. Machine guns
20 million dead
Armistice Nov 11 1918
Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, triggered the war.
Trench warfare, poison gas, and machine guns made the Western Front a hellish stalemate.
The Armistice on November 11, 1918, ended fighting but left a broken Europe ripe for future conflict.

title: Russian Revolution
hook: Two revolutions. One year. Empire gone.
bullets: Tsar executed with his family
Lenin: Peace Land Bread
USSR born 1922
Civil war killed millions
Divided the world 70 years
Two revolutions in 1917 overthrew the tsar and brought the Bolsheviks to power under Lenin.
The Romanov family was executed in 1918, ending centuries of imperial Russian rule.
The USSR formed in 1922 and became a global superpower that shaped the 20th century.
credit: unknown; photo retake by George Shuklin · Public domain

title: Roaring Twenties
hook: Jazz. Flappers. Then it all CRASHED.
bullets: Women got the vote — 1920
Prohibition = speakeasies
Louis Armstrong & jazz
Flappers broke every rule
Crashed Oct 1929
The 19th Amendment granted American women the right to vote in 1920.
Prohibition from 1920 to 1933 banned alcohol and fueled a booming underground speakeasy culture.
The stock market crash of October 1929 ended the decade and ushered in the Great Depression.

title: Discovery of Penicillin
hook: Mold in a dish saved BILLIONS.
bullets: Fleming — 1928 accident
Killed bacteria instantly
Mass-produced for WWII
Launched antibiotic era
Superbugs today
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident in 1928 when mold contaminated a petri dish.
Scientists Florey and Chain later developed methods to mass-produce the antibiotic for WWII.
Penicillin launched the antibiotic era and saved countless lives from bacterial infections.
credit: Science Museum London / Science and Society Picture Library · CC BY-SA 4.0

title: Great Depression
hook: One crash. A decade of HELL.
bullets: Black Tuesday — Oct 29 1929
25% unemployment
Hoovervilles everywhere
Dust Bowl destroyed farms
WWII ended it
Black Tuesday on October 29, 1929, saw the stock market lose billions in a single day.
Unemployment in the United States eventually reached roughly 25 percent.
Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal programs provided relief, recovery, and lasting reforms like Social Security.

title: World War II
bullets: 70-85 million dead
Holocaust — 6 million Jews
Pearl Harbor 1941
D-Day — largest invasion
Japan surrendered 1945
World War II killed an estimated 70 to 85 million people, the deadliest conflict in human history.
The Holocaust systematically murdered six million Jews and millions of other victims.
Allied victory in 1945 reshaped the global order and ushered in the nuclear age.
credit: US Coast Guard, photo 26-G-2517 · Public domain

title: D-Day
hook: 156000 troops. One day. The longest day.
bullets: June 6 1944 — Normandy
5 beaches. 156000 troops
Omaha = bloodiest
Fooled Hitler
Average age: 26
Allied forces landed on five Normandy beaches on June 6, 1944, in the largest amphibious invasion ever.
Omaha Beach saw the heaviest American casualties of the entire operation.
D-Day opened the Western Front and began the liberation of Nazi-occupied Europe.
credit: US Coast Guard, photo 26-G-2517 · Public domain

title: The Holocaust
bullets: 6 million Jews murdered
Death camps: Auschwitz
Final Solution — Wannsee 1942
Resistance in ghettos
Never again
Nazi death camps like Auschwitz, Treblinka, and Sobibor were built for industrial-scale murder.
The Wannsee Conference in 1942 coordinated the 'Final Solution' to exterminate European Jews.
Allied liberation of the camps in 1945 revealed horrors that led to the promise of 'Never again.'

title: Indian Independence
bullets: Gandhi — peaceful resistance
Independence Aug 15 1947
Partition: India + Pakistan
10-20 million displaced
Largest democracy born
Mahatma Gandhi led India to independence through nonviolent civil disobedience and mass protest.
India gained independence on August 15, 1947, but was simultaneously partitioned into India and Pakistan.
The partition displaced 10 to 20 million people and killed an estimated 1 to 2 million.
credit: British Information Services, an agency of the British Government, rest… · Public domain

title: Cold War and Space Race
hook: Two superpowers. 60000 nukes. Zero direct war.
bullets: Sputnik — 1957
Gagarin — first in space
Moon landing — July 1969
Cuban Missile Crisis 1962
Gave us GPS & satellites
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, shocking the West and starting the Space Race.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961, and Neil Armstrong walked the Moon in 1969.
The Cold War rivalry also drove advances in satellites, computing, and nuclear technology.

title: Civil Rights Movement
hook: They said sit down. She said NO.
bullets: Rosa Parks — 1955
MLK: I Have a Dream
Brown v Board
Civil Rights Act — 1964
Voting Rights Act — 1965
Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955.
Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech at the March on Washington in 1963.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 dismantled legal segregation.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
hook: A wall divided a city for 28 YEARS.
bullets: Built 1961
140+ died trying to cross
Reagan: Tear down this wall
Nov 9 1989 — gates opened
Hammers not bullets
East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop citizens from fleeing to the West.
Ronald Reagan famously demanded in 1987: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'
On November 9, 1989, crowds surged through opened gates and began tearing the wall apart.
credit: Unknown photographer, Reproduction by Lear 21 at English Wikipedia . · CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Invention of the Internet
bullets: ARPANET — 1969
First message: LO
World Wide Web — 1989
Dot-com boom
5 billion people online
ARPANET, the military precursor to the internet, sent its first message in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, making the internet accessible to all.
Today more than five billion people around the world are connected online.

title: End of Apartheid
hook: 27 years in prison. Then he became PRESIDENT.
bullets: Apartheid was South Africa's legal system of racial segregation (1948-1994).
Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison for anti-apartheid activism.
International boycotts and sanctions pressured the white minority government.
Mandela was released in 1990 and negotiated a peaceful transition.
First democratic elections held April 27, 1994 — Mandela became president.
At age 75, he chose reconciliation over revenge.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission addressed past atrocities.
South Africa's transition is studied as a model of peaceful revolution.

title: Building the Great Pyramids
bullets: Built circa 2560 BCE for Pharaoh Khufu
Each block weighed roughly 2.5 tons
Workforce likely paid laborers not slaves
Aligned to cardinal points with stunning precision
Still among the largest structures ever built
The Great Pyramid of Giza originally stood 481 feet tall and was the world's tallest structure for nearly 4,000 years.
Archaeologists believe a skilled workforce of thousands — not slaves — built the pyramids over roughly 20 years.
The pyramids were designed as elaborate tombs to ensure the pharaoh's safe passage to the afterlife.

title: Hammurabi's Code
bullets: Carved on a 7-foot stone stele circa 1754 BCE.
One of the oldest written legal codes
Punishments scaled by social class
Famous principle: eye for an eye
Displayed publicly so no one could claim ignorance.
Hammurabi was the sixth king of Babylon and ruled from approximately 1792 to 1750 BCE.
The code included detailed laws on trade, family, property, and criminal punishment.
Its principle of proportional justice influenced legal systems across the ancient Near East.

title: Battle of Thermopylae
bullets: Fought August 480 BCE at a narrow mountain pass.
King Leonidas led roughly 300 Spartans
Held off Xerxes' massive Persian army for three days.
Betrayed when a local showed Persians a secret path.
Became the ultimate symbol of heroic last stands.
The Spartan stand at Thermopylae bought critical time for Greece to organize its defenses.
The Greek historian Herodotus recorded the battle, blending history with enduring legend.
A monument at the site honors the Spartans who obeyed their laws and stayed to fight.

title: Alexander the Great
bullets: King of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE.
Never lost a battle in 15 years of campaigning.
Created an empire from Greece to India
Founded 20 cities named Alexandria
Died in Babylon cause still debated today
Alexander was tutored by Aristotle and carried a copy of the Iliad on his campaigns.
He founded Alexandria in Egypt, which became a great center of learning and culture.
His vast empire fragmented into rival Hellenistic kingdoms after his death at age 32.
credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Public domain

title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
bullets: Murdered March 15 44 BCE the Ides of March.
At least 60 senators plotted against him
Stabbed 23 times in the Senate
Last words debated: Greek or Latin phrase
His death ended the Roman Republic forever
Caesar's dictatorship for life alarmed senators who feared the return of monarchy.
Marc Antony's funeral speech turned public opinion against the assassins.
Caesar's heir Octavian eventually defeated his killers and became Emperor Augustus.

title: Fall of the Roman Empire
bullets: Western Empire fell officially in 476 CE
Barbarian general Odoacer deposed last emperor Romulus
Economic crisis inflation and tax collapse
Massive barbarian migrations overwhelmed borders
Eastern Byzantine Empire survived another millennium
Rome's fall was a gradual process of economic decline, military pressure, and political instability.
The sack of Rome by Visigoths in 410 CE shocked the ancient world.
The Eastern Roman Empire at Constantinople survived for another thousand years.

title: Spartacus Slave Revolt
bullets: Began 73 BCE when gladiators escaped Capua
Spartacus a Thracian gladiator led the rebellion
Army grew to 70,000 escaped slaves
Defeated multiple Roman legions for two years
Crucified 6,000 survivors along Appian Way
Spartacus was a former gladiator who became the most feared rebel leader in Roman history.
The revolt threatened Rome's entire social order built on slavery.
Crassus and Pompey ultimately crushed the rebellion and claimed the glory.
credit: Carole Raddato from FRANKFURT, Germany · CC BY-SA 2.0

title: Cleopatra's Egypt
bullets: Last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt
Spoke nine languages including Egyptian
Allied with Julius Caesar then Mark Antony
Died by snake bite or poison 30 BCE.
Her death ended 3,000 years of pharaonic rule.
Cleopatra was the last pharaoh of Egypt and a shrewd political strategist.
She aligned Egypt with Rome through relationships with Caesar and Mark Antony.
After her defeat, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
bullets: Crossed Alps in 218 BCE with war elephants.
Led Carthage against Rome in Second Punic War.
Crushed Romans at Battle of Cannae
Wandered Italy 15 years without taking Rome
Eventually defeated at Battle of Zama
Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with war elephants remains one of history's boldest military maneuvers.
At Cannae he destroyed a Roman army nearly twice the size of his own.
Scipio Africanus finally defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE.

title: The Trojan War
bullets: Described in Homer's Iliad circa 8th century BCE.
Archaeological site of Troy found in modern Turkey.
Helen of Sparta sparked the legendary conflict
Greeks used Trojan Horse trick to enter city.
Blurred line between myth and history for millennia.
Homer's Iliad and Odyssey immortalized the Trojan War for Western civilization.
Archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann excavated Troy in the 1870s.
The war symbolizes the blurred line between ancient myth and historical memory.
credit: Sosias (potter, signed). Painting attributed to the Sosias Painter (nam… · Public domain

title: Death of Socrates
bullets: Executed 399 BCE for corrupting Athenian youth
Chose hemlock over exile
Taught Plato who taught Aristotle
Never wrote a word himself
His trial defined philosophy forever
Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens.
He chose to drink hemlock rather than accept exile from his beloved city.
His student Plato preserved his teachings, shaping Western philosophy forever.

title: The Terracotta Army
bullets: Discovered 1974 by farmers digging a well
Guards tomb of China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang.
Each figure has unique facial features
Originally painted in bright colors
Represents real army formations and weapons
The terracotta warriors were buried to protect Qin Shi Huang in the afterlife.
An estimated 8,000 life-sized figures have been discovered so far.
The site near Xi'an remains one of the greatest archaeological finds of the 20th century.

title: Great Wall of China
bullets: Construction began over 2,000 years ago
Not one wall but many sections and dynasties.
Built to repel northern nomadic invaders
Estimated millions of workers died building it
Longest human-made structure on Earth
The Great Wall was built and rebuilt by multiple Chinese dynasties over centuries.
It stretches over 13,000 miles across northern China's rugged terrain.
Today it stands as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and symbol of Chinese civilization.

title: The Silk Road
bullets: Trade network linking China to Mediterranean
Silk spices paper and ideas flowed both ways.
Buddhism spread from India to East Asia
Marco Polo traveled it in the 13th century.
Declined when sea routes opened in 15th century.
The Silk Road connected merchants, monks, and travelers across thousands of miles.
Paper, gunpowder, and Buddhism spread along its ancient trade routes.
Marco Polo's travels along the Silk Road opened European eyes to Asia's riches.
credit: Whole_world_-_land_and_oceans_12000.jpg : NASA/Goddard Space Flight Cen… · Public domain

title: Mayan Civilization Collapse
bullets: Peak between 250 and 900 CE in Mesoamerica.
Built pyramids calendars and writing system
Predicted eclipses with stunning accuracy
Classic collapse still debated by archaeologists
Drought warfare and overpopulation likely causes
The Maya built sophisticated cities with pyramids, observatories, and advanced calendars.
Their writing system was the most developed in the pre-Columbian Americas.
The Classic Maya collapse around 900 CE remains one of archaeology's great mysteries.

title: Aztec Empire
bullets: Capital Tenochtitlan built on a lake
Ruled central Mexico from 1428 to 1521
Practiced ritual human sacrifice to sun god
Market of Tlatelolco served 60,000 daily
Fell to Hernan Cortes and allied tribes
Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world when the Spanish arrived.
Aztec engineers built canals, causeways, and floating gardens on a lake.
Spanish conquest and European diseases devastated the Aztec population within decades.
credit: Badseed based on work by historicair which in turn was based on Madman2… · CC BY-SA 3.0

title: Inca Empire
bullets: Largest empire in pre-Columbian Americas
Capital Cusco high in Andes Mountains
Built Machu Picchu without iron tools
Quipu knot system recorded data without writing
Fell to Francisco Pizarro in 1533
The Inca ruled an empire of roughly 10 million people without a written language.
They built Machu Picchu and an extensive road network high in the Andes.
Spanish conquistadors captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa and seized their gold.
credit: Pedro Szekely at https://www.flickr.com/photos/pedrosz/ · CC BY-SA 2.0

title: Stonehenge Mystery
bullets: Constructed 3000-2000 BCE on Salisbury Plain
Some stones dragged 150 miles from Wales
Aligned with summer and winter solstices
Purpose debated: temple calendar or burial site
Built by people without metal tools or wheels.
Stonehenge was built in stages between 3000 and 2000 BCE on England's Salisbury Plain.
Some bluestones were transported over 150 miles from Wales.
The monument aligns with the summer and winter solstices.

title: Rosetta Stone
bullets: Discovered 1799 by French soldiers in Egypt
Same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphics demotic Greek.
Jean-Francois Champollion cracked code 1822
Opened 3,000 years of Egyptian history
Now displayed at British Museum London
The Rosetta Stone was the key that unlocked the mystery of Egyptian hieroglyphics.
It bears the same decree written in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek scripts.
Jean-François Champollion cracked the code in 1822 after years of study.

title: Pompeii Eruption
bullets: Mount Vesuvius erupted in August 79 CE, burying the Roman city of Pompeii.
Volcanic ash preserved bodies, buildings, and graffiti in extraordinary detail.
City of 11,000 buried under 20 feet of ash.
Pliny the Younger witnessed the eruption and left a vivid written account.
Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748, frozen in time beneath the ash.
Mount Vesuvius erupted on August 24, 79 CE, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash.
The ash preserved buildings, artifacts, and haunting body casts for centuries.
Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748 and offers a frozen snapshot of Roman daily life.

title: Library of Alexandria
bullets: Founded 3rd century BCE in Egypt
May have held 400,000 scrolls and manuscripts
Center of ancient science and philosophy
Destroyed in stages over centuries
Loss of knowledge still mourned today
The library was founded in the 3rd century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt.
Scholars like Euclid and Archimedes may have studied and worked there.
Its destruction — whether by fire, war, or neglect — remains one of history's greatest losses of knowledge.

title: Phoenician Alphabet
bullets: Developed circa 1050 BCE in modern Lebanon
First widely used phonetic alphabet
Spread via Phoenician maritime trade network
Ancestor of Greek Latin and Arabic scripts
Made literacy accessible beyond scribes
The Phoenician alphabet had just 22 characters, all representing consonant sounds.
Phoenician traders spread their script across the Mediterranean world.
Greek, Latin, Arabic, and Hebrew writing systems all trace roots to Phoenician letters.

title: Battle of Marathon
bullets: Athenians defeated Persian invasion 490 BCE
Outnumbered Greeks used disciplined phalanx
Legendary runner Pheidippides collapsed after
His run inspired modern marathon distance
Saved Western democracy at the brink
The Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE halted the first Persian invasion of Greece.
The hoplite phalanx formation proved decisive against Persia's larger force.
The legend of Pheidippides running to Athens inspired the modern marathon race distance.

title: Qin Shi Huang Unification
hook: One emperor. One China. BURNED the books.
bullets: First emperor unified China 221 BCE
Built early Great Wall and terracotta army
Standardized writing currency and measurements
Ordered burning of Confucian texts
Obsessed with immortality and mercury pills
Qin Shi Huang unified warring Chinese states under one empire in 221 BCE.
He standardized weights, measures, currency, and writing across China.
His tomb complex with the terracotta army reflects his obsession with immortality and power.
credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Public domain

title: Roman Colosseum
bullets: Completed 80 CE under Emperor Titus
Hosted gladiator fights and mock sea battles
Free admission to Roman citizens via bread and circuses.
Estimated 400,000 died in arena over centuries
Still stands as icon of Roman engineering
The Colosseum could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.
Gladiators, wild animals, and mock naval battles entertained Roman crowds.
It remains one of Rome's most iconic landmarks nearly 2,000 years later.

title: Constantine and Christianity
bullets: Roman emperor from 306 to 337 CE
Legalized Christianity with Edict of Milan 313
Founded Constantinople as new capital
Called First Council of Nicaea 325 CE
Shifted Rome from pagan to Christian empire
Constantine legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE.
He founded Constantinople as a new capital of the Roman Empire.
His conversion helped transform Christianity from persecuted faith to imperial religion.
credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France · Public domain

title: Attila the Hun
hook: Scourge of God. Rome FEARED him.
bullets: Led Hunnic Empire across Europe 434-453 CE
Demanded half the Western Roman Empire as tribute.
Invaded Gaul and Italy sacking cities
Died on wedding night cause disputed
His death ended major Hunnic threat to Rome.
Attila led the Hunnic Empire across Europe in the mid-5th century CE.
Both the Eastern and Western Roman Empires paid him tribute to avoid invasion.
His sudden death in 453 CE ended the greatest Hunnic threat to Rome.

title: Boudica's Revolt
hook: She burned London to the GROUND.
bullets: Celtic queen of Iceni tribe in Britain
Romans flogged her and raped her daughters
Led army that destroyed Colchester and London
Killed 70,000 Romans and allies
Defeated then poisoned herself to avoid capture
Queen Boudica of the Iceni tribe led a massive uprising against Roman rule in 60-61 CE.
Her forces burned Colchester, London, and St. Albans before facing defeat.
She remains a powerful symbol of resistance and Celtic identity in Britain.

title: Ashoka the Great
bullets: Mauryan emperor of India 268-232 BCE
Kalinga War deaths horrified him into peace
Spread Buddhism across Asia via edicts
Built pillars with earliest readable Indian script
One of history's greatest rulers of compassion
Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire in India from roughly 268 to 232 BCE.
The carnage of the Kalinga War horrified him and turned him toward Buddhism.
His edicts on pillars across India promoted nonviolence, tolerance, and moral governance.
credit: Photo Dharma from Sadao, Thailand · CC BY 2.0

title: Destruction of Carthage
bullets: Third Punic War ended 146 BCE
Scipio Aemilianus razed city over 17 days
Survivors sold into slavery
Legend says Rome sowed fields with salt
Removed Rome's greatest Mediterranean rival
Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE after the Third Punic War.
The city was razed and its territory became the Roman province of Africa.
The legend that Rome salted the earth may be myth, but Carthage was utterly erased.
credit: Patrick Verdier, Free On Line Photos · Copyrighted free use

title: Minoan Eruption of Thera
bullets: Massive eruption circa 1600 BCE near Crete
Devastated advanced Minoan civilization
Possibly inspired Atlantis legend
Tsunami hit Crete 100 miles away
One of largest volcanic events in human history.
A volcano may have erased Atlantis.
The events surrounding Minoan Eruption of Thera reveal how quickly history can turn on a single decision.
From classrooms to documentaries, Minoan Eruption of Thera remains a staple of history storytelling.

title: Oracle of Delphi
hook: Kings traveled WEEKS for her words.
bullets: Priestess Pythia delivered prophecies for centuries
Sitting over volcanic fumes caused trance states
Consulted before wars and founding cities
Croesus of Lydia and Alexander the Great visited.
Closed by Christian emperor Theodosius 393 CE
Empires rose and fell on her riddles.
The events surrounding Oracle of Delphi reveal how quickly history can turn on a single decision.
From classrooms to documentaries, Oracle of Delphi remains a staple of history storytelling.

title: Egyptian Mummification
bullets: Process took 70 days for elite Egyptians
Brain removed through nose with hooks
Heart left in body as seat of the soul.
Canopic jars held liver lungs stomach intestines
Believed necessary for afterlife journey
Death was just the beginning.
Archaeologists and historians continue to uncover new evidence about Egyptian Mummification.
Ancient sources and modern science together help us reconstruct the world of Egyptian Mummification.
